newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece hit by new wave of strikes.
newsitem.headline: Greece hit by new wave of strikes.

text.p: Greece's socialist government faced a new wave of strikes on Monday with a 48-hour walkout by public servants, a strike by teachers and threats by militant farmers to block national roads again.
The strike in the public sector forced state hospitals and public companies to operate on skeleton staffs while elementary school teachers joined a week-long strike by teachers in high schools.
Some 5,000 people marched through the streets of Athens to parliament to demand higher salaries and pensions,causing traffic chaos in Athens for three hours.

Prime Minister Costas Simitis has drawn up a strict 1997 budget, described as the toughest in 15 years, and announced tight new incomes and tax policies, saying the country needs bitter medicine to turn its ailing economy around.

Farmers, who blocked national roads with tractors for 25 days in December, threatened to repeat their protest starting on Tuesday if their demands for higher price supports, cheaper fuel and tax cuts were not met.
The government has sent thousands of riot police to central Greece to prevent a new blockade but farmers seemed unmoved by warnings that riot police would be used if necessary to keep the roads open.

"We don't want a clash with police. It won't be easy for them to attack us when we are on our tractors ... They have batons, we have our tractors and it will be thousands of us," farmers' leader Yannis Patakis said in an interview with the Athens daily Eleftherotypia.
Patakis said he expected some 5,000 tractors to block five key junctions in central Greece which would "cut Greece in half".
Simitis successfully stared down the farmer's blockade in December but this time warned that farmers who would attempt to block roads would be arrested and prosecuted.

Thousands of police sent from Athens and the northern city of Salonika have occupied many hotels in the central town of Larissa, the headquarters of the farmers' protest, while a police helicopter has been monitoring farmers' rallies in Larissa and other nearby farm towns.
"Our target is a total blackout with thousands of cars (stranded). Everything will stop," Patakis said.
